I think the earth is flat. More than most SF founders believe in their own startups. I don't actually think the earth is flat. What I love is the person who does, and won't move no matter how much the world laughs, argues, or shows them proof. I don't admire being wrong. I admire a belief that survives being alone. Anyone can believe when the launch works, the room claps, and the numbers go up. You need the belief that stays when all of that disappears and everything goes to shit. That kind of conviction changes how you talk too. People ramble when they're still negotiating with themselves. Jargon, caveats, five minutes to say one thing, because they haven't actually decided what they believe. When you know something from every angle, the words get short. That is why I have not posted in almost two weeks. I had a vision. But it didn't feel like mine. I was looking for the belief underneath everything I want to build and say. Finding it was brutal. But I have mine now. 📸 : startup talk with Pratham Patel and Collin Hickey

PLOT TWIST: VC-backed startups commit more fraud than bootstrapped startups. At first, this sounds like a founder problem. But the research suggests the system may play a role too. • Startups founded during overheated funding markets were 19% more likely to commit fraud later. • Investor’s unrealistic expectations can push founders toward bad decisions. • Founder-controlled boards were linked to roughly 2x the fraud risk. That’s what caught my attention. The interesting part isn’t just who commits fraud. → It’s whether fundraising sometimes rewards confidence more than accuracy. → It’s whether the system meant to find ambitious founders can also reward founders willing to exaggerate. And AI could make this worse. Fake demos, dashboards, testimonials, and product interactions are now much easier to create. I went down the rabbit hole on the research, how startup fraud actually develops, and why VC may be creating its own version of an old economic problem. If you’re raising money, investing in startups, or building in the AI boom, this is worth understanding. Check it out here: https://lnkd.in/gdjdUGxw

I just wrapped up my SWE internship at Apple . This Summer, I worked at Apple Pay in NYC, focusing on privacy and security around Apple Pay analytics – feeds that shape senior leaders’ decisions to launch, grow, or sunset products. I’ve worked in finance analytics before, but Apple was unique: remarkably customer-obsessed and exceptionally talent-dense. Apple engineers target perfection. Nothing goes live without rigorous design reviews and cross-team debate, ensuring every solution is optimal and highly reliable. After a summer building live, high-throughput async pipelines processing thousands of events a second, I’ve matured as an engineer. Months of debating and refining my design and implementation gave me the confidence to challenge and question engineers far more senior than me. I loved being an integral presence in stakeholder meetings and a source of truth. Beyond the technical skills in distributed systems I developed, Apple has taught me to insist on the highest standards, and I’m really grateful to my team for pushing me to grow: Chukwuebuka Ononiwu, Nick Loukas, Pavel Frolov , and the rest. Thanks to everyone along the way, and I'll be sharing more about my next steps soon!
